results.result: TGFBR2 is constitutively expressed in retinal microglia and endothelial cells. Immunohistochemical analysis showed TGFBR2 expression in CX3CR1+ microglia and CD31+ endothelial cells in both IPL and OPL (C28, C29). RNAseq data confirmed high Tgfbr2 mRNA expression in microglia but low expression in other retinal neurons in adult mouse retina (C30), and high expression in both microglia and endothelial cells in postnatal mouse brain (C31, C32).
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C32 are well-supported by converging evidence from immunohistochemistry (Figure 1A) and published RNAseq datasets (Figures 1B-C). The protein and mRNA expression data are consistent and establish baseline TGFBR2 expression patterns in relevant cell types.

results.result: Tamoxifen-induced Cre recombination specifically ablated TGFBR2 in retinal microglia. Genomic DNA analysis showed significant loss of exon 4 in CD11b+ microglia from TMX-treated TG animals but not in control groups or non-microglial cell types (C33, C34). This was confirmed at the mRNA level by rtPCR showing reduced exon 4-containing transcripts in flow-sorted microglia (C35).
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C35 demonstrate successful and specific genetic ablation using appropriate controls (untreated TG, TMX-treated controls) and multiple cell populations (microglia, endothelial, other retinal cells). The qPCR data (Figure 1D-E) provide strong evidence for microglia-specific TGFBR2 deletion.

results.result: TGFBR2 ablation induced progressive morphological transformation of retinal microglia. Microglia showed slight deramification at 1 day (C36), marked reduction in ramification at 2-5 days (C37), and transition to elongated morphology by 3-10 weeks (C38). Elongated microglia adhered closely to retinal blood vessels (C39), while controls remained unchanged (C40). Morphologically transformed microglia were also found in the avascular subretinal space (C41), suggesting cell-autonomous changes rather than vessel-induced effects (C42).
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C42 are supported by detailed time-course immunohistochemical analysis (Figure 2, Videos 1-2, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B). The observation of transformed microglia in the avascular subretinal space (C41) provides strong evidence for the cell-autonomous interpretation (C42), though alternative explanations are not fully excluded.

results.result: TGFBR2 ablation increased microglial numbers through proliferation. Flow cytometry showed significant increases in CD11b+ microglia at 3 and 10 weeks post-TMX (C43). Cell counting confirmed increased densities in all retinal laminae (IPL, OPL, SRS) (C44), corresponding to emergence of Ki67+ proliferating microglia (C45). Ki67 was absent in subretinal microglia (C46), suggesting migration from inner layers (C47).
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C47 are supported by converging evidence from flow cytometry (Figure 3B) and immunohistochemistry (Figure 3C-D). The inference about migration (C47) is reasonable given the absence of Ki67 in subretinal microglia, though direct migration tracking was not performed.

results.result: Increased microglial numbers arose from resident microglia, not monocyte infiltration. Cell-fate mapping showed all IBA1+ cells expressed tdTomato 4 months post-TMX, indicating no monocyte contribution (C48). Morphologically changing cells were P2RY12+ and Ki67+ in the first week (C49), indicating proliferation and modification of pre-existing endogenous microglia (C50).
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C50 are well-supported by cell-fate mapping (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) and P2RY12/Ki67 immunohistochemistry (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D). The experimental design appropriately distinguishes resident microglia from infiltrating monocytes using established markers and sufficient time for monocyte turnover.

results.result: TGFBR2 ablation reduced microglial process complexity and retinal coverage. Individual microglia showed marked reductions in branch points (C51) and dendritic field area (C52). Despite increased density, the proportion of retina lacking microglial coverage was significantly greater (C53), likely diminishing microglia-synapse contact and supportive functions (C54).
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C53 are supported by quantitative morphological analysis (Figure 3E-H). The inference about diminished supportive functions (C54) is reasonable given the reduced coverage and prior literature on microglia-synapse interactions, though direct functional measurements were not provided.

results.result: TGFBR2 ablation downregulated microglial sensome gene expression. qRT-PCR showed markedly reduced mRNA levels of Cx3cr1, P2yr12, Tmem119, and Siglech in flow-sorted microglia from TG animals (C55). In vitro TGFβ ligand administration to cultured WT microglia upregulated Tmem119 and Siglech (C56). Protein-level analysis confirmed reduced Cx3cr1-driven EYFP fluorescence (C57) and decreased TMEM119 immunopositivity (C58).
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C58 are well-supported by converging evidence from in vivo qRT-PCR (Figure 4A), in vitro ligand stimulation (Figure 4B), and protein-level analyses (Figure 4C-F). The in vitro experiments (C56) provide mechanistic support for direct TGFβ regulation of sensome genes.

results.result: TGFBR2 ablation selectively decreased expression of microglial growth factors. mRNA expression of Bdnf and Pdgfa decreased following TGFBR2 ablation, while Igf1 was unchanged (C59, C60). TGFβ ligands increased expression of these growth factors in cultured retinal microglia (C61).
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C61 are supported by qRT-PCR data from flow-sorted microglia and cultured cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1). The selective effects on different growth factors suggest specificity in TGFβ signaling regulation.

results.result: TGFBR2 ablation induced microglial activation and a proinflammatory phenotype. qRT-PCR showed upregulated mRNA expression of activation markers (H2-Aa, Cd68, Cd74), chemotactic cytokines (Ccl2, Ccl8), and Apoe (C62-C64). Cultured WT microglia showed decreased ApoE and Ccl2 with TGFβ ligands (C65). Immunohistochemistry confirmed increased protein expression of CD68, MHCII, CD74, F4/80, and CD45 (C66, C67). RT-PCR showed progressive upregulation of macrophage-enriched transcripts (Saa3, Pf4, Cd5l) (C68).
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C68 are strongly supported by converging evidence from qRT-PCR (Figure 5A), in vitro experiments (Figure 5B), immunohistochemistry (Figures 5C-F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), and RT-PCR (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G). The data consistently demonstrate a shift toward an activated, proinflammatory microglial phenotype.

results.result: TGFBR2-deficient microglia induced secondary Müller cell gliosis with neurotoxic characteristics. Radial GFAP immunopositivity emerged at 5 days and persisted at 10 weeks (C69), colocalizing with GS+ Müller cell processes (C70). GFAP mRNA levels increased at 2 weeks and persisted at 8 weeks (C71). Progressive upregulation of A1 neurotoxic astrocytic gliosis genes occurred, while A2 neuroprotective genes were unchanged (C72, C73).
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C73 are supported by immunohistochemistry (Figures 2, 6A), qPCR (Figure 6B), and RT-PCR analysis (Figure 6C). The selective upregulation of A1 over A2 genes is particularly notable, though the functional consequences of this specific gliosis pattern require further validation.

results.result: TGFBR2 ablation caused progressive retinal thinning and neuronal loss. OCT imaging showed total retinal thickness decreased to 95% at 3 weeks and 80% at 10 weeks (C74), with contributions from both inner and outer retina (C75). Histological analysis confirmed decreased thickness in multiple retinal layers (C76). Densities of BRN3A+ retinal ganglion cells and cone arrestin+ cone photoreceptors decreased significantly (C77). TUNEL+ apoptotic nuclei appeared in all retinal nuclear layers (C78).
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C78 are well-supported by converging evidence from in vivo OCT imaging (Figure 7A-B), histological analysis (Figure 7C-D), immunohistochemistry (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), and TUNEL assay (Figure 7E-F). The progressive nature and multi-layer involvement indicate widespread neurodegeneration.

results.result: TGFBR2 ablation impaired retinal function, particularly synaptic transmission. ERG showed significantly reduced dark-adapted rod responses, with b-wave amplitudes more reduced than a-wave amplitudes (C79, C80). Light-adapted cone responses showed reduced b-wave but unchanged a-wave amplitudes (C81). Decreased b-to-a amplitude ratios for both dark- and light-adapted responses (C82) indicated rod photoreceptor dysfunction and loss of synaptic transmission in both rod and cone pathways (C83).
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C83 are supported by comprehensive ERG analysis (Figure 7G-H). The differential effects on a-wave vs. b-wave amplitudes provide strong evidence for synaptic dysfunction (C83), consistent with prior literature on microglial depletion effects. Statistical analysis using 2-way ANOVA is appropriate.

results.result: Molecular profiling revealed neuroinflammatory pathway activation following TGFBR2 ablation. Hierarchical clustering showed similar profiles between control groups with/without TMX (C84, C85), but significant differences in TMX-treated TG animals (C86). Significantly upregulated genes included microglial activation markers, proinflammatory cytokines, complement components, and inflammatory response regulators (C87-C90). Early downregulation of Cx3cr1 was detected at 2 weeks (C91). GO analysis revealed differential involvement of neuroinflammatory signaling and NFAT-mediated signaling pathways (C92).
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C92 are supported by comprehensive Nanostring mRNA profiling (Figure 8A-C). The analysis includes appropriate controls (n=3 per group) and uses established bioinformatics approaches. The finding that tamoxifen alone has no major effect (C85) is important for interpretation.

results.result: TGFBR2 ablation in microglia did not affect normal retinal vascular structure. Fluorescein angiography at 12 weeks post-TMX showed intact blood-retina barrier with no vascular leakage or perfusion changes (C94). Histological analysis showed normal arrangement of endothelial cells and pericytes, lacking signs of spontaneous neovascularization (C95).
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C95 are supported by fluorescein angiography (Figure 9A) and immunohistochemical analysis (Figure 9B). This finding is important for distinguishing microglial-specific effects from endothelial TGFBR2 effects reported in prior literature.

results.result: TGFBR2-deficient microglia showed exaggerated responses to laser injury and promoted choroidal neovascularization. In a laser-induced CNV model, TG mice showed increased recruitment of Iba1+ microglia/macrophages to injury sites (C96), associated with larger RPE defects and increased CNV size (C97). These findings indicate that while microglial TGFBR2 is dispensable for normal vasculature maintenance (C98), TGFBR2-deficient microglia can potentiate pathological neovascularization when inducing factors are present (C99).
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C99 are supported by laser injury model data (Figure 9C-F) with appropriate quantification (40 lesions from 6 animals per group). The interpretation that microglial TGFBR2 is dispensable for normal vasculature (C98) but important for injury responses (C99) is well-supported by the combined data from C94-C97.

results.result: Constitutive TGFβ signaling maintains microglial organization through direct and indirect mechanisms. The study demonstrates that TGFβ signaling is necessary for maintaining microglial organization (C111). The authors propose that TGFβ can serve as a direct homeostatic signal (C112) and that sensome gene products enable microglia to orient to environmental cues (C113). Downregulation of Cx3cr1 and P2ry12 may render microglia less responsive to CX3CL1 and ATP (C114).
results.evaluation: Claim C111 is well-supported by the experimental data showing disorganization following TGFBR2 ablation. Claims C112-C114 are reasonable mechanistic interpretations based on the data and prior literature, though they represent speculative reasoning rather than directly tested hypotheses. The proposed mechanisms are plausible but would benefit from additional functional validation.

results.result: TGFBR2 ablation induced transition of resident microglia to a proinflammatory phenotype without monocyte infiltration. Loss of TGFβ signaling was accompanied by microglial proliferation and increased expression of activation markers (C119), indicating transition from homeostatic to proinflammatory phenotype (C120). Cell-fate mapping and P2RY12 analysis showed this alteration was predominantly from resident microglia (C121) without monocyte infiltration (C122). The absence of monocyte infiltration may relate to intact blood-retinal barrier and absence of empty myeloid cell niche (C123, C124).
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C122 are well-supported by experimental data (Figures 3, 5, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-D). The mechanistic explanations for absence of monocyte infiltration (C123, C124) are speculative but reasonable, supported by citations to relevant literature. This finding differs from brain studies and highlights tissue-specific differences.

results.result: Transformed microglia acquired CD206 expression but perivascular macrophages did not substantially contribute. Retinal microglia gradually acquired CD206 immunopositivity following TMX (C125). However, prominent proliferation and migration of baseline CD206+ perivascular macrophages were not detected, indicating minimal contribution to the transformed cell population (C126).
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C126 are supported by time-course immunohistochemical analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2). The interpretation that perivascular macrophages do not substantially contribute (C126) is reasonable given the lack of observed proliferation/migration, though more definitive lineage tracing would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: TGFBR2-deficient microglia perturbed neuroinflammation regulation through Müller cell interactions. The altered microglial phenotype perturbed neuroinflammation regulation (C127), which is mediated partly by microglia-Müller cell interactions (C128). Gliotic changes in Müller cells were spatiotemporally coincident with microglial changes (C129) and featured selective upregulation of neurotoxic A1 astrocytic gliosis genes (C130), indicating potential neurotoxic influence from Müller cells (C131). These Müller cell changes may feedback onto microglia via secreted signals (C132).
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C131 are supported by experimental data (Figures 2, 6) and citations to relevant literature. The spatiotemporal coincidence (C129) and selective A1 gene upregulation (C130) provide strong evidence for the proposed interactions.
